metadata.title: Examining student ICT use and learning outcomes: Evidence from Japanese PISA data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for Japan and analyzes it with the R package intsvy, which is designed to respect PISA’s complex two-stage sampling design. The authors explicitly state that intsvy uses replicate weights provided in the dataset and uses all plausible values for the three assessed learning domains (reading, mathematics, science). This implies survey-weighted estimation rather than a simple unweighted regression, and standard errors reflect the replicate-weight approach. The analytic sample is restricted by missingness at the variable level (e.g., some ICT-use and competence variables have small missing proportions), and the paper reports that missing values are handled via listwise deletion within the intsvy workflow.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Japanese PISA 2018 data for 15-year-old students. The paper reports that the dataset contains 6109 observations overall, with variable-specific missingness (e.g., ICT-use and ICT-competence indices have small missing counts). The main intsvy regressions use all plausible values for reading, mathematics, and science and apply listwise deletion as part of the intsvy estimation workflow; thus, the effective N differs by outcome and ICT-use form (e.g., N≈5922–6012 across Table 2).

top_predictors: ICT use outside of school for leisure (ENTUSE)
ICT use outside of school for schoolwork (HOMESCH)
main_findings.performance_metrics: intsvy regression coefficients (Table 2) with PVs; interaction terms (Table 3). No ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Japan) the study leveraged perceived ICT competence and multiple ICT-use forms (ENTUSE, HOMESCH, ICTCLASS, ICTOUTSIDE) to predict reading achievement (PVs), finding that leisure ICT use outside school is negatively associated with reading while subject-related ICT use during and outside lessons is positively associated. This indicates that promoting supervised, subject-related ICT use in classrooms and for learning tasks outside lessons may support reading outcomes, whereas unsupervised leisure ICT use may be detrimental.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Japan) the study leveraged perceived ICT competence and multiple ICT-use forms (ENTUSE, HOMESCH, ICTCLASS, ICTOUTSIDE) to predict mathematics achievement (PVs), finding that leisure ICT use outside school is negatively associated with mathematics while subject-related ICT use during and outside lessons is positively associated. This indicates that mathematics gains are more likely when ICT is used for subject-related learning activities rather than for leisure, and that ICT competence moderates these associations across the distribution.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Japan) the study leveraged perceived ICT competence and multiple ICT-use forms (ENTUSE, HOMESCH, ICTCLASS, ICTOUTSIDE) to predict science achievement (PVs), finding that leisure ICT use outside school is negatively associated with science while subject-related ICT use during and outside lessons is positively associated. This indicates that science education policies should emphasize structured, learning-focused ICT integration (e.g., supervised inquiry or mini-laboratory uses) rather than allowing ICT time to be dominated by entertainment.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes Japanese PISA 2018 microdata (15-year-olds; Japan only) to examine how five forms of student ICT use relate to reading, mathematics, and science achievement. The authors estimate 15 PV-based regression models using the R package intsvy, which accounts for PISA’s complex design via replicate weights and uses all plausible values for each domain; they also run unconditional quantile regression (UQR) using the first plausible value to assess heterogeneity across the achievement distribution. Across mean results, ICT use for leisure outside school is consistently negatively associated with all three outcomes, while subject-related ICT use during and outside lessons is positively associated with all three outcomes. Interaction results show that the direction/magnitude of associations varies by perceived ICT competence, and quantile results indicate stronger effects at distribution tails for some ICT-use forms. Limitations include cross-sectional (correlational) design and listwise deletion for missing data within the intsvy workflow.
